quote:
Meta just made agentic AI a little less theoretical.

Its new Muse agent can move from WhatsApp into connected apps. Send emails. Book travel. Sell your stuff. Move your money.

@AIatMeta actually delayed the launch after internal testing turned up security and reliability problems. The version that shipped this week comes with permission controls, plus a separate safety agent that watches everything Muse does.

That tells you where the hard part of agentic AI is actually moving.

Picture asking an agent to book a flight for Friday.

It checks your calendar. Searches fares. Picks a flight. Hits the payment screen.

The airline receives a perfectly valid transaction from your account.

From the airline's side, none of this is clear.

Did you approve that specific purchase? Did you give the agent a general travel budget? Was the permission only good for today? Could it change the destination if it found a better deal? What happens if it spends more than expected?
For most of the internet era, authentication tried to answer one question: is this really you?
Passwords, two-factor authentication, biometrics, and KYC all grew out of that same problem.
Agentic systems raise a second question.
Did you authorize this machine to do this specific thing?

That creates three layers of trust.

The human behind the account. The agent performing the action. And the authority connecting the two.

The third layer is the hard part.

A useful agent can't stop and ask for approval before every small move. Give it too little authority and automation loses most of its value. Give it broad, standing authority, and one bad model, one bug, or one misread instruction can suddenly reach your inbox, your calendar, your files, and your money.

The fallout goes past security.

Banks will need to know when an agent was actually authorized to spend. Merchants will need proof when a transaction gets disputed. Insurers will need to work out who's liable. Platforms will need a way to kill delegated authority instantly. Regulators will eventually want an audit trail back to the one human who started the chain.

This is where proof of personhood gets interesting in an AI-heavy internet.

The system doesn't need to prove an agent is human. It needs to prove one real, unique person sits behind that agent's authority, while keeping that person's privacy intact and revealing only the permission needed for that one action.

AI agents are going to run thousands of actions on our behalf eventually.

The infrastructure underneath all of it will have to remember something simple: who gave permission, what they were allowed to do, and when that permission ran out.

quote:
📰 #imNEWS: @Meta launched Muse, a personal AI agent that talks like a chat in the Muse app or WhatsApp, powered by Muse Spark. It runs in a dedicated Muse Secure VM, can keep working after you close the app, and asks before emails or purchases. Link by Stripe covers agent checkout with one-time cards. US rollout on iOS, Android, and https://t.co/gSNkgq6rfh, free for most use, with subscriptions for more.

🔑 3 Key Takeaways

① An agent that keeps working
Muse is built for everyday tasks (email, travel) and bigger goals. Share a goal, it builds a plan, then it can open a browser, fill forms, and negotiate. For longer jobs it keeps going after you close the app and comes back when something changes or it needs approval.

② A dedicated VM, not a chat overlay
Muse Secure VM is a contained cloud computer for the agent plus your data and credentials. A separate Sentinel agent has to approve anything that hits the internet. Muse cannot see passwords or payment methods. A Confidential VM later this year encrypts the whole box with a key only the user holds.

③ Checkout and memory with limits
Muse can pay with Link, including purchase protections and one-time cards. Shop Pay and 1Password support are coming. It can turn a saved Instagram recipe reel into a grocery list and remember dietary restrictions. You pick app access, can disconnect anytime, and can opt out of training.

✅ Action Item
Run one real task in Muse this week (book something, dispute a bill, or checkout). Write down where it asked for approval vs acted on its own. If you sell via WhatsApp or Instagram, that log is your map for how consumer agents will sit between you and the customer.
